q: After a defense verdict in a federal products-liability suit over a collapsed extension ladder, the plaintiff moves for a new trial and submits a juror’s affidavit stating: (1) during deliberations Juror 6, a retired carpenter, told the others that in his 30 years on job sites, ladders like this one failed only when overloaded; (2) Juror 2 brought a printout of the ladder’s online customer reviews, which praised its sturdiness, into the jury room and read it aloud; and (3) after hearing the reviews, two jurors changed their votes to find for the defendant. Which parts of the affidavit may the court consider?
o: Item 2 only.
Items 2 and 3, because once extraneous information is shown, the court needs to know whether it actually changed the outcome.
Items 1 and 2, because both brought information from outside the trial record into deliberations.
None of them, because each describes something that happened during deliberations and the Peña-Rodriguez exception is limited to racial bias.
e: Rule: 606(b) bars juror testimony about deliberations, effects on votes, and mental processes. Exceptions: extraneous prejudicial information, outside influence, a verdict-form mistake (plus Peña-Rodriguez racial bias). A juror’s own experiences are internal (Warger).
oe: Correct. Online reviews are information from outside the trial that reached the jury improperly, so 606(b)(2)(A) lets a juror testify that it happened. Item 1 is a juror drawing on his own life experience, which is internal (Warger). Item 3 describes the effect of something on jurors’ votes, which 606(b)(1) bars even when an exception applies; the court decides prejudice objectively, without asking jurors how they voted.

The exception opens the door only to whether extraneous information reached the jury. 606(b)(1) still forbids testimony about “the effect of anything on that juror’s or another juror’s vote.” Courts judge the likely effect on a hypothetical average juror instead.

Warger draws the line by the nature of the information, not by whether it was in the record. A juror’s own experience is something jurors bring with them, so it is internal even when it is specific and influential.
606(b)(2) has its own textual exceptions apart from Peña-Rodriguez. Extraneous prejudicial information, an outside influence, and a mistake on the verdict form may all be proved by juror testimony.

q: A woman is charged with aiding and abetting a killing and claims she acted in fear for her and her son’s lives. She testifies that the deceased had bragged to her about beating two men so badly that they ended up in the hospital. The prosecution suggests in cross-examination that she made the stories up. She then offers certified police reports showing that the deceased did hospitalize two men in exactly the beatings she described. She concedes she never saw the reports before the killing. The prosecution objects that the reports are irrelevant. How should the court rule?
o: Overrule the objection, because the reports corroborate her testimony about what he told her, which bears on her fear.
Sustain the objection, because she never saw the reports, so they could not have affected her fear.
Overrule the objection, because the reports show the deceased’s violent character, which is an essential element of self-defense under Rule 405(b).
Sustain the objection, because her own testimony about what he told her is the only permissible evidence of her state of mind.
e: Rule: 401: relevance can run through corroboration. In James, police reports she never saw were relevant to her testimony about her state of mind, though 403 remained available.
oe: Correct. This is United States v. James (en banc). The trial judge asked whether the reports were relevant to her state of mind, and they weren’t, since she never saw them. The right question was whether they were relevant to her testimony about her state of mind, and they were: if the beatings really happened, it’s more likely he told her about them and less likely she invented the stories. Rule 403 remains available (Judge Kleinfeld’s dissent).
That was the trial court’s framing, which the en banc court rejected. Relevance can run through corroboration of her account of what he told her, even though the reports themselves never reached her.

A victim’s violent character is not an essential element of self-defense; what matters is the defendant’s reasonable fear. Specific acts don’t come in under 405(b) for that reason. The reports are relevant for a different, non-character purpose: corroboration.
No rule limits proof of state of mind to the defendant’s own words. Any evidence with a tendency to make her account more or less probable is relevant under 401.
topic: Relevance (401, 402, 104) — FRE 401 · United States v. James

q: A home health aide is charged with murdering an elderly diabetic patient with an insulin overdose. She testifies that the patient must have injected himself twice by mistake. After giving pretrial notice, the prosecution offers evidence that in the past three years two other patients in the aide’s care suffered unexplained insulin overdoses, one of them fatal. She was never charged in either incident. How should the court rule on her objection?
o: Admit it to show absence of accident, because so many unexplained overdoses among one caregiver’s patients are unlikely to be innocent.
Exclude it, because she was never charged or convicted in the earlier incidents, so the jury would be trying uncharged crimes.
Admit it under Rule 404(a)(2), because a defendant who claims accident puts her character for carefulness in issue.
Exclude it, because the doctrine of chances still asks the jury to infer that she is the kind of person who harms patients.
e: Rule: 404(b)(2) absence of accident and the doctrine of chances: repeated unusual “accidents” are objectively improbable. No conviction is needed (Huddleston); 403 and notice still apply.
oe: Correct. This is the doctrine of chances (Rex v. Smith; United States v. Woods). The inference turns on how improbable the coincidence is rather than on what kind of person she is, and 404(b)(2) lists absence of mistake and lack of accident. The judge must still balance under 403 and give a 105 instruction on request.
Other-act evidence needs no charge or conviction. Under Huddleston the question is whether a jury could reasonably find, by a preponderance, that the acts happened and she did them.
Claiming accident doesn’t open a character exception. 404(a)(2)(A) applies only when the defendant offers her own pertinent trait. This evidence comes in, if at all, around the box under 404(b)(2).

Scholars debate whether the doctrine of chances escapes propensity, but courts have long accepted it as proof of absence of accident (Rex v. Smith, the brides in the bath). It isn’t barred per se; 403 does the screening.
topic: Other acts (404(b)) — FRE 404(b)(2) · doctrine of chances

q: A guest slips on a polished marble lobby floor on a rainy evening and sues the hotel for negligence. A week after the fall, the hotel began putting out non-slip runner mats whenever it rains. At trial the hotel’s general manager testifies, “That lobby was as safe as it could possibly be on a rainy night. There was nothing more we could have done.” The plaintiff then offers evidence of the runner mats. How should the court rule?
o: Admit it to impeach the manager and to show feasibility, which he put in dispute, but not as proof of negligence.
Exclude it, because Rule 407 bars evidence of subsequent remedial measures for every purpose.
Admit it to prove negligence, because the manager opened the door by vouching for the hotel’s safety, so the hotel can’t invoke Rule 407.
Exclude it, because the mats were a change in policy rather than a physical repair of the floor itself.
e: Rule: 407: post-accident measures can’t prove negligence, culpable conduct, a defect, or the need for a warning, but may be admitted to impeach or, if disputed, to prove ownership, control, or feasibility.
oe: Correct. 407 bars subsequent remedial measures only when offered to prove negligence or culpable conduct. The court may admit them for impeachment or, if disputed, to prove feasibility. “Nothing more we could have done” does both, much like the class hypo where the restaurant’s claim of a $40,000 repair let in its $55.26 receipt.
407 is a limited exclusion. Its second sentence lists permitted purposes, including impeachment and disputed feasibility. Rule 410 is the specialized rule that bars evidence for nearly all purposes.
Opening the door doesn’t change the purpose for which the jury may use the evidence. It comes in for impeachment and feasibility only, and the hotel is entitled to an instruction saying so.
407 covers any “measures” that would have made the harm less likely, including new policies, warnings, and procedures, not just physical repairs.

q: A bar patron sues another patron for battery, claiming the defendant hit him with a beer bottle without provocation. The defendant, who says he never threw a punch, calls his longtime neighbor to testify that the defendant has a reputation in the neighborhood as a peaceful, gentle man. The plaintiff objects. How should the court rule?
o: Sustain the objection, because the exceptions that let a defendant offer his own pertinent trait apply only in criminal cases.
Overrule the objection, because reputation is a proper way to prove character under Rule 405(a).
Overrule the objection, because a battery claim alleges a crime, so he may defend his good name as an accused could.
Sustain the objection, because reputation testimony is hearsay.
e: Rule: The 404(a)(2)(A)–(C) exceptions apply only in criminal cases (2006 amendment). In a civil case, character offered to prove conduct is barred.
oe: Correct. 404(a)(2) applies only in criminal cases. The 2006 amendment rejected decisions like Perrin v. Anderson, which had let civil defendants facing quasi-criminal charges offer good character. In a civil battery suit the evidence is barred by 404(a)(1).
405(a) governs how character is proved once some rule lets it in. It doesn’t create a right to offer character. Here no exception applies, so the method never comes into play.
That was the reasoning of Perrin v. Anderson, which the 2006 amendment rejected. The “special dispensation” belongs only to criminal defendants, whose liberty is at stake.
Reputation testimony about character is admissible over a hearsay objection under FRE 803(21). The problem is 404(a)(1), not hearsay.
topic: Character and habit (404(a), 405, 406) — FRE 404(a)(2) · civil cases

q: Right after a rear-end collision, Driver A walks to Driver B’s window and says, “Are you hurt? I’ll pay for your ER visit. I’m so sorry; I was looking at my GPS.” Two months later, B’s lawyer sends A a letter demanding $25,000. A’s lawyer disputes both fault and the amount. At a settlement meeting, A says, “Fine, I wasn’t watching the road, but $25,000 is absurd. I’ll pay $7,000.” Talks fail and B sues. Which of A’s statements may B introduce to prove A was negligent?
o: “I’m so sorry; I was looking at my GPS” only.
“I’ll pay for your ER visit” and “I was looking at my GPS.”
“I was looking at my GPS” and “I wasn’t watching the road.”
None of them, because every statement concerned the same claim and the parties later tried to settle it.
e: Rule: 409 excludes only offers to pay medical expenses, not statements made with them. 408 excludes offers and statements made in compromise negotiations over a disputed claim.
oe: Correct. The offer to pay the ER visit is excluded by 409, but 409 reaches only the offer itself, not statements made with it, so the apology and admission at the scene come in. Everything A said at the settlement meeting, both the admission and the $7,000 offer, falls under 408 because it was said in compromise negotiations over a disputed claim.
Offering to pay medical expenses is exactly what 409 excludes when offered to prove liability. Only the accompanying statement of fault survives.

The second admission was made during compromise negotiations after a demand and a dispute over fault and amount. 408(a)(2) excludes conduct or statements made in those talks, not just the dollar offer. This is broader than 409.
The later negotiations don’t reach back to protect A’s statements at the scene. No claim was disputed then, and 409 protects only the offer to pay medical expenses.
topic: Compromise and medical expenses (408, 409) — FRE 409 · FRE 408

q: A diner owner is charged with setting fire to a rival restaurant. To prove motive, the prosecution calls the rival’s owner, who testifies that two days before the fire he told a newspaper he planned to open a second restaurant directly across the street from the defendant’s diner. The prosecution shows that the article ran the next morning and that the defendant subscribed to the paper. The defendant testifies that he never reads it. The defense objects that the rival’s plan is irrelevant unless the defendant knew about it. What should the judge do?
o: Admit the testimony if a reasonable jury could find, by a preponderance, that the defendant knew of the plan.
Decide herself under Rule 104(a) whether the defendant more likely than not read the article, and exclude the testimony unless she is persuaded.
Exclude the testimony, because the defendant’s sworn denial creates a factual dispute that makes the evidence speculative.
Admit the testimony without any showing of knowledge, because a rival’s plans are always relevant to motive.
e: Rule: 104(b) conditional relevance: admit if a reasonable jury could find the conditional fact by a preponderance. The judge doesn’t weigh credibility (Huddleston, Cox).
oe: Correct. This is conditional relevance under 104(b), as in Cox. The judge doesn’t weigh credibility or make her own finding (Huddleston). She asks only whether a jury could reasonably find the conditional fact. The subscription and the article’s timing are enough, as Cox’s near-daily visits to Hammer’s mother’s house were in that case.
104(a) is for preliminary questions such as privilege and competency. When relevance depends on a fact, 104(b) applies, and the jury decides whether the fact exists.
A denial doesn’t defeat conditional relevance. If a reasonable jury could find knowledge, the evidence comes in and the jury weighs the denial.
The plan supplies a motive only if the defendant knew about it. That is the missing link 104(b) exists to police, and without a sufficient showing the evidence should be excluded or struck.

q: Under investigation for bank fraud, a loan officer asks to meet the FBI case agent. At the meeting he asks, “If I tell you where the money went, can you get me a deal?” The agent answers that only the prosecutor can make deals but that he will pass along anything useful. The officer then describes how he routed the funds. Weeks later, in plea negotiations with the Assistant U.S. Attorney that break down, he admits forging two signatures. He later pleads guilty but is allowed to withdraw the plea. At trial, which of these may the government offer in its case-in-chief?
o: His statements to the FBI agent about routing the funds.
His admission to the AUSA that he forged the signatures.
His withdrawn guilty plea.
None of them, because all of his statements were made in an effort to obtain leniency.
e: Rule: 410 bars withdrawn guilty pleas, nolo pleas, Rule 11 statements, and statements in plea talks with a prosecuting attorney. Statements to agents without authority aren’t covered.
oe: Correct. 410(a)(4) protects statements made in plea discussions “with an attorney for the prosecuting authority.” Statements to an agent without authority to bargain aren’t covered (Greene), and the agent told him so, which defeats any claim under the Robertson test that he reasonably expected to be negotiating a plea.
That statement was made in plea discussions with the prosecutor that didn’t produce a guilty plea, so 410(a)(4) bars it against him in the case-in-chief.
410(a)(1) bars a guilty plea that was later withdrawn. Letting the jury hear it would defeat the purpose of allowing the withdrawal.
Hoping for leniency doesn’t make a conversation a plea discussion. 410 protects talks with the prosecuting attorney, not unilateral overtures to police.
topic: Pleas and insurance (410, 411) — FRE 410(a)(4) · statements to agents

q: A defendant is charged with possessing cocaine with intent to distribute. His defense is that the drugs were for his personal use. He offers to stipulate that police found 360 individually wrapped packets of cocaine in his car and asks the court to bar the prosecution from showing the jury the packets or photographs of them. The prosecution refuses the stipulation. How should the court rule?
o: Let the prosecution use the packets, because Old Chief’s stipulation rule is limited to proof of the defendant’s legal status.
Bar the evidence, because the stipulation removes the issue from the case and makes the physical evidence irrelevant.
Bar the evidence, because Old Chief requires the prosecution to accept any stipulation conceding those facts.
Admit the evidence, because Rule 403 doesn’t apply to physical evidence seized from the defendant.
e: Rule: 403: a stipulation doesn’t make evidence irrelevant. Old Chief requires accepting a stipulation only when the issue is the defendant’s legal status; otherwise parties choose their own proof.
oe: Correct. Old Chief reaffirmed that a party ordinarily chooses its own proof, citing descriptive richness, a morally reasonable verdict, and jurors’ expectations. Its holding covers felon status, where the name of the crime adds nothing but prejudice. Here the quantity and packaging bear directly on intent to distribute, the disputed issue.
A fact need not be disputed for evidence of it to be relevant (ACN to Rule 401; Old Chief). The question is whether 403 calls for exclusion, and it doesn’t here.
That overreads Old Chief, which limited its holding to proof of legal status. Outside that setting, the prosecution may tell its story with its own evidence.
403 applies to all relevant evidence. The point is that the danger of unfair prejudice here doesn’t substantially outweigh strong probative value.
topic: Rule 403 and 105 — FRE 403 · Old Chief · stipulations

q: A bookkeeper charged with embezzlement calls a coworker, who testifies that in her opinion the bookkeeper is an honest person. On cross, the prosecutor, who has the former employer’s termination letter in hand, asks, “Did you know he was fired from his last job for padding his expense reports?” The coworker says no. The prosecutor then offers the former employer’s HR director to testify about the padding. Which ruling is correct?
o: Allow the question but exclude the HR director’s testimony.
Allow both, because the defendant opened the door to his character for honesty.
Exclude both, because the defendant was never charged or convicted for the padding.
Exclude the question, because an opinion witness may be asked only “Have you heard...?” and not “Did you know...?”
e: Rule: 405(a): character is proved by reputation or opinion. On cross of the character witness, specific instances may be asked about with a good-faith basis (Michelson), but there’s no extrinsic proof.
oe: Correct. Once a defendant offers his own pertinent trait under 404(a)(2)(A), 405(a) allows cross-examination of the character witness about relevant specific instances, here to test the basis of her opinion, if the prosecutor has a good-faith basis (Michelson). Specific acts may be raised only on cross, though, and the questioner must take the answer. Proving the padding through the HR director would be extrinsic evidence of a specific act.

Opening the door lets the prosecution rebut, but under 405(a) rebuttal witnesses are limited to reputation or opinion. Specific instances may be raised only on cross-examination of the character witness.
Michelson allowed questions about an arrest, which proves less than a conviction does. What’s required is a good-faith basis, and the termination letter supplies one.

Under 405(a), the old “have you heard” (reputation) versus “do you know” (opinion) distinction no longer controls admissibility. Both forms are allowed so long as the question tests the witness’s basis.

q: A client sues a licensed massage therapist for battery, alleging he sexually assaulted her during a session. Twenty days before trial, she discloses that she will call two other former clients, who will testify that he assaulted them in the same way during sessions. Neither reported it to police, and he was never charged. He moves to exclude their testimony. How should the court rule?
o: Admit it under Rule 415 for any relevant purpose, including propensity, subject to ordinary Rule 403 balancing.
Exclude it, because Rules 413 through 415 apply only in criminal prosecutions, where the defendant’s liberty is at stake.
Exclude it unless the other assaults resulted in convictions or at least formal charges.
Admit it automatically, because Congress has decided that propensity evidence in sexual-assault cases outweighs any prejudice.
e: Rule: 413/414/415: in sexual-assault and child-molestation cases (415 for civil cases), the party’s other such acts are admissible for any relevant purpose, including propensity. No conviction is needed, ordinary 403 applies, and disclosure is due 15 days before trial.
oe: Correct. 415 applies Rules 413 and 414 in civil cases based on sexual assault or child molestation (Carroll v. Trump is a recent example). No charge or conviction is needed; the threshold is presumably Huddleston’s. Disclosure at least 15 days before trial was satisfied. Under Guardia, the 403 balance is the ordinary one.
Rule 415 exists specifically for civil cases involving a claim of sexual assault or child molestation.
Rep. Molinari’s floor statement says the past offense need not have produced a conviction. The Huddleston preponderance-sufficiency standard governs.
Rule 403 still applies; that is why Mound upheld Rule 413 against a due-process attack. Guardia requires a normal 403 weighing, neither tilted for nor against admission.

q: A defendant is charged with robbing a convenience store at knifepoint. The clerk’s identification is shaky, and the defense is misidentification. The prosecution offers the defendant’s conviction, four years earlier, for robbing a gas station at knifepoint, arguing that it proves identity. How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because a knifepoint robbery is too common a method to show that one person committed both crimes.
Admit it, because identity is disputed and both crimes were armed robberies of small stores committed with knives.
Admit it, because a conviction is reliable proof that the earlier robbery happened.
Admit it, because identity is one of the exceptions to the propensity ban listed in Rule 404(b)(2), and identity is disputed here.
e: Rule: 404(b) identity (modus operandi) requires signature-level similarity, not prosaic commonalities (Trenkler vs. Pisari). The listed purposes aren’t exceptions.
oe: Correct. Identity through modus operandi requires similarities so distinctive that the crime “could not be anyone else’s” (Trenkler). A single prosaic commonality like a knife isn’t enough (Pisari). Without a signature, the only route to identity is that he robbed before, so he robbed again, which is the forbidden inference.
A dispute over identity makes identity a proper purpose but doesn’t make every similar crime probative of it. The likeness must be idiosyncratic, not generic.
Reliability of proof answers the Huddleston question, whether the other act happened. It doesn’t supply a non-propensity reason the act is relevant.
The 404(b)(2) purposes are not exceptions. They are non-character routes to relevance, and a chain that runs through the propensity box is still barred (Zackowitz; Kirsch).

q: In a civil suit over a bar fight, the plaintiff calls an eyewitness who testifies that she saw the defendant swing a pool cue at the plaintiff. The defense’s cross-examination asks only about the lighting and her distance from the pool table. The plaintiff then calls the eyewitness’s neighbor to testify that the eyewitness has an excellent reputation in the neighborhood for truthfulness. The defense objects. How should the court rule?
o: Sustain the objection, because truthful character can be supported only after it has been attacked.
Overrule the objection, because Rule 608(a) lets any party support a witness’s credibility with reputation evidence.
Overrule the objection, because the defense’s cross-examination challenged the eyewitness’s credibility.
Sustain the objection, because Rule 608 applies only to criminal defendants who testify.
e: Rule: 608(a): evidence of truthful character comes in only after an attack on character for truthfulness. Attacks on perception or bias don’t count, and bolstering is improper.
oe: Correct. Under 608(a), support comes only after an attack. Questions about lighting and distance attack her perception, the “that’s an error” mode of impeachment, not her character for truthfulness. Offering good character now is bolstering (Problem 4.1).
608(a) allows support, but its last sentence limits evidence of truthful character to after an attack on character for truthfulness.

Not every challenge to credibility is an attack on character for truthfulness. Doubting perception, bias, or a single contradiction usually doesn’t open the door to good-character evidence (Problem 4.6).
608 applies to every witness, in civil and criminal cases alike, unlike 404(a)(2).

q: A defendant is charged with distributing cocaine. In its case-in-chief, the government offered his three-year-old felony conviction for possessing cocaine for sale under Rule 404(b), and the judge excluded it under Rule 403. The defendant then testifies and denies the charge. On cross-examination, the government offers the same conviction under Rule 609(a)(1)(B). The defendant argues that because the conviction failed the more lenient 403 test, it must fail 609’s stricter test as well. How should the court respond?
o: Reject the argument and weigh the conviction anew, because 609 measures its bearing on truthfulness, not on guilt.
Exclude the conviction, because once the court finds evidence fails Rule 403, that ruling binds it for the rest of the trial.
Admit the conviction without weighing, because a testifying defendant’s felony convictions are automatically admissible.
Admit the conviction under ordinary Rule 403, because the defendant chose to testify.
e: Rule: 609(a)(1)(B): a testifying accused’s felony comes in only if its probative value on truthfulness outweighs its prejudicial effect to him. That’s a separate question from the 404(b)/403 ruling (Valencia).
oe: Correct. This is Problem 4.4 (United States v. Valencia, 8th Cir.). The 404(b)/403 ruling measured probative force on substantive guilt; the 609(a)(1)(B) ruling measures probative force on truthfulness. Losing one doesn’t dictate the other, and appellate courts defer to the trial judge on both. (Whether a drug conviction says much about honesty is fair to question.)
An in limine or case-in-chief ruling under one rule doesn’t control a later ruling for a different purpose under another rule.
Only crimen falsi convictions under 609(a)(2) come in without balancing. A testifying defendant’s other felonies go through 609(a)(1)(B)’s special balance.
403 governs non-defendant witnesses under 609(a)(1)(A). For an accused, the conviction comes in only if probative value outweighs prejudicial effect to the defendant.

q: A defendant is charged in federal court with sexual assault and claims he wasn’t the attacker. The examining nurse found bruising and abrasions consistent with intercourse. By written motion filed a month before trial, the defense seeks to offer (1) testimony that the complainant had intercourse with her boyfriend several hours before the alleged assault, to explain the injuries, and (2) testimony that she “was sleeping around with several men” that month. Which ruling is correct?
o: Item 1 may be admitted under Rule 412(b)(1)(A) after an in camera hearing, but item 2 is barred.
Both are barred, because Rule 412 excludes all evidence of a victim’s other sexual behavior in a criminal case.
Both are admissible, because a defendant claiming misidentification may offer any evidence about other possible sources of the injury.
Item 1 is admissible only if the prosecutor offers it, because the accused may not offer evidence under Rule 412(b)(1)(A).
e: Rule: 412(b)(1)(A): in criminal cases, specific instances may show another source of semen, injury, or physical evidence; general conduct stays barred. 412(c) requires a written motion 14 days before trial and an in camera hearing.
oe: Correct. 412(b)(1)(A) permits specific instances of a victim’s sexual behavior offered to show that someone other than the defendant was the source of semen, injury, or other physical evidence, and the motion followed 412(c)’s procedure (written motion at least 14 days before trial, notice, in camera hearing). Item 2 is general conduct or predisposition, not a specific instance, so it is barred (compare Walker, Problem 5.2).
412(b)(1) has three criminal-case exceptions, and explaining the source of physical evidence is the first.
Only specific instances qualify. General evidence of sexual activity with others is exactly the inference 412 was designed to block.
The source-of-physical-evidence exception is typically invoked by the defense. The “offered by the prosecutor” language belongs to 412(b)(1)(B), on sexual behavior with the accused.

q: A defendant is charged with burglarizing a jewelry store on a Monday night. On Thursday, two officers responding to a neighbor’s noise complaint knock on the door of the defendant’s apartment building. When they ask the defendant, who is on the front steps, whether he lives there, he runs. The prosecution offers his flight as evidence of consciousness of guilt of the burglary. Which is the defense’s strongest argument for excluding it?
o: Nothing shows he knew he was a burglary suspect when he ran, so the flight says little about guilt of this crime.
Flight is character evidence showing he is the kind of person who runs from police, so Rule 404(a)(1) bars it.
Commonwealth v. Warren makes evidence of flight from police inadmissible as a matter of law.
The prosecution must first prove beyond a reasonable doubt that he was fleeing rather than simply leaving.
e: Rule: Flight rests on four links: the behavior was flight, flight shows consciousness of guilt, of this crime, and so actual guilt. Attack the weak link and argue 403 (Warren: there are other reasons to flee).
oe: Correct. Flight evidence depends on a chain of inferences: (1) the behavior was flight; (2) flight shows consciousness of guilt; (3) of this crime; (4) so actual guilt. Here link 3 is weakest. The flight came three days later, from officers asking about a noise complaint, and he had no reason to think they were there about the burglary (Thelma & Louise clip). Commonwealth v. Warren adds other reasons people run from police.
Flight isn’t offered to show a character trait. It’s conduct offered to show his state of mind about a particular crime. The proper attack is on the inferential chain and under 403.
Warren, a Massachusetts case, held that flight may carry little weight and that a qualified community witness may explain other reasons for it. It didn’t create a rule excluding flight evidence.
Preliminary facts of this kind are at most 104(b) questions, which require evidence sufficient to support a finding. No beyond-a-reasonable-doubt threshold applies.

q: A Haitian-born defendant is convicted in state court of drug distribution. After the verdict, two jurors sign affidavits. Both recount that during deliberations a third juror said, “People from the islands all run drugs. That’s all I need to know to convict him.” One affidavit adds that another juror remarked at some point that the defendant’s accent was “hard to follow.” The defendant moves for a new trial. What should the court do?
o: Consider the “islands” statement, because a clear statement of reliance on ethnic stereotypes to convict overrides the no-impeachment rule.
Refuse to consider either statement, because racial bias is not “extraneous prejudicial information” under the state’s version of Rule 606(b).
Order a new trial on the strength of both statements, because any comment about the defendant’s ethnicity or national origin taints the verdict.
Refuse to consider the statements, because the jurors affirmed their impartiality in voir dire, so the only remedy is the Warger two-step test for voir-dire dishonesty.
e: Rule: Peña-Rodriguez: a clear statement that a juror relied on racial or ethnic stereotypes or animus to convict a criminal defendant must be considered despite 606(b). Offhand remarks don’t qualify.
oe: Correct. Peña-Rodriguez holds that when a juror makes a clear statement showing reliance on racial stereotypes or animus to convict a criminal defendant, the court must be allowed to consider it. The remark about the accent is an offhand comment that doesn’t show animus as a significant motivating factor, so it doesn’t meet the threshold.
That was Colorado’s position, which the Supreme Court reversed. The exception rests on the Sixth Amendment, not on 606(b)’s text.

Peña-Rodriguez set a threshold: a clear statement and animus as a significant motivating factor. Offhand comments don’t qualify, and even a qualifying statement leads to a hearing, not an automatic new trial.
Warger concerns proving a juror lied in voir dire, and juror testimony about deliberations can’t be used for that. The racial-bias exception is separate, and the voir dire answers don’t defeat it.

q: On June 3, a child breaks an ankle landing in the foam pit at a trampoline park. On July 1, the park installs a padded border around the pit. On August 12, a second child is injured in the same pit despite the new border, and the second child’s family claims the pit itself was too shallow. Both families sue the park for negligence, and each wants to prove the July 1 installation to show that the park knew the pit was dangerous. Rule 407 bars the evidence in which suit?
o: Only the first child’s suit.
Both suits, because the border was installed in response to an accident at the same pit.
Neither suit, because the park’s knowledge is a permitted purpose under Rule 407.
Only the second child’s suit, because the border failed to prevent the second injury.
e: Rule: 407 applies only to measures taken after the plaintiff’s own injury. A measure taken between two accidents is barred in the first plaintiff’s suit only (Wolf Attack).
oe: Correct. 407 applies to measures taken after the injury that would have made “an earlier injury” less likely. The July border came after the first child’s injury but before the second child’s, so as to the second child it isn’t a subsequent remedial measure (Problem 2.1, Wolf Attack: the chaining was barred in the beagle owner’s suit but not in Daniel’s). In the second suit the court applies 401 and 403.
407 measures time against the plaintiff’s own injury. A measure taken before that plaintiff was hurt isn’t “subsequent” as to that plaintiff.
Knowledge of danger is just another way of saying culpable conduct or negligence, which 407 bars. The permitted purposes are impeachment and, if disputed, ownership, control, or feasibility.
That reverses the timing. The measure followed the first injury, which is the suit in which 407 applies.
topic: Remedial measures (407) — FRE 407 · timing · Wolf Attack

q: An undercover officer buys heroin from a man in a hooded jacket on a dark street corner. The defendant is arrested an hour later with no drugs or marked money on him. At trial, the defense concedes that whoever made the sale knew the substance was heroin and intended to sell it; the only issue is whether the defendant was the seller. The prosecution offers the defendant’s prior conviction for selling heroin, arguing that it shows “knowledge of the drug trade” and “intent.” How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because with knowledge and intent conceded, the prior sale bears on identity only through propensity.
Admit it, because knowledge is a permitted purpose listed in Rule 404(b)(2).
Admit it, because intent is an element of every distribution charge, and a not-guilty plea keeps it in issue.
Admit it, but only if the prior conviction is less than ten years old.
e: Rule: 404(b): the non-propensity purpose must bear on an issue actually in dispute. “Knowledge” or “intent” can’t be a label for propensity reasoning toward identity.
oe: Correct. This is Problem 3.2 (Drug Seller). A 404(b)(2) purpose must connect to a fact actually in issue. With knowledge and intent conceded, labeling the evidence “knowledge” just disguises the propensity chain to identity. 403 would also weigh heavily against it.
Listing a purpose doesn’t make it relevant in a given case. Where knowledge isn’t contested, the evidence has no non-propensity probative value on that point.
The defense has expressly conceded that the seller intended to sell. With that concession, the only live issue is identity, and the prior sale reaches identity only through character.
The ten-year limit belongs to Rule 609(b), which governs impeachment by conviction. It has nothing to do with substantive other-act evidence under 404(b).

q: At a murder trial, the defense concedes the victim’s death, its cause, and the number of stab wounds; the only issue is identity. The prosecution offers (1) a crime-scene photograph of the wounds, which the medical examiner uses to explain that their angle shows a left-handed attacker (the defendant is left-handed), and (2) three color autopsy photographs of the victim’s internal organs, which no witness refers to. The defense objects to both under Rule 403. Which ruling is most defensible?
o: Admit photograph 1 and exclude the autopsy photographs.
Exclude all of them, because the defense conceded the death, its cause, and the wounds.
Admit all of them, because photographs of the victim are always relevant to the fact and cause of death in a murder case.
Exclude photograph 1 as cumulative of the medical examiner’s testimony and admit the autopsy photographs.
e: Rule: 403: weigh probative value on contested issues against unfair prejudice. Concessions lower probative value (Bocharski: the angle-and-depth photos came in; the unexplained autopsy photos didn’t).
oe: Correct. This tracks Bocharski. Concessions lower a photo’s probative value on the conceded points but don’t eliminate its value on contested ones. Photo 1 bears directly on identity, the disputed issue. The autopsy photos, tied to no testimony, serve mainly to inflame, so their slight value is substantially outweighed by unfair prejudice.
A concession doesn’t make evidence irrelevant (ACN to 401). Photo 1 is probative of the one disputed issue, the attacker’s identity, through the angle of the wounds.
Relevance isn’t the end of the analysis. Where those facts are conceded and the photos are unexplained, 403 exclusion is appropriate (Bocharski Exhibits 46–47).
Photo 1 illustrates and supports the examiner’s key inference. If anything is needlessly cumulative or inflammatory here, it’s the autopsy photos.

q: After a warehouse fire destroys a tenant’s inventory, the tenant sends the landlord a letter demanding $400,000 and blaming the landlord’s old wiring. The landlord denies fault. During the settlement talks that follow, the landlord hires an electrical consultant to inspect the building and prepare a report for use in the negotiations. The report concludes that the wiring violated the electrical code. Talks collapse, the tenant sues, and the tenant obtains the report and offers it to prove the wiring was defective. How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because the report is a statement made during compromise negotiations.
Admit it, because the report was written by an outside consultant rather than by the landlord or its lawyers.
Admit it, because Rule 408 protects only offers of money, not factual findings made along the way.
Admit it, because no lawsuit had been filed when the consultant prepared the report.
e: Rule: 408(a)(2): conduct or statements made during compromise negotiations over a disputed claim, including an agent’s report prepared for the talks, can’t prove validity or amount. The claim needn’t have been filed.
oe: Correct. This is Problem 2.4 (Hotel Inspection). A report prepared by the party’s agent for use in the settlement process counts as a statement made “during compromise negotiations.” Otherwise parties would be afraid to hire such consultants. 408 doesn’t make the underlying facts undiscoverable, so the tenant can hire its own expert.
The consultant acted as the landlord’s agent in the negotiation process. 408 protects statements made in the course of negotiations, whoever the speaker is.
408(a)(2) expressly covers “conduct or a statement made during compromise negotiations.” Since 2006 that has included factual admissions.
408 requires a disputed claim, not a filed complaint. The demand letter and the landlord’s denial created one.
topic: Compromise and medical expenses (408, 409) — FRE 408(a)(2) · Hotel Inspection (Problem 2.4)

q: A defendant charged with assault claims the alleged victim attacked first. He calls a witness who testifies that the victim has a reputation for violence. In rebuttal, the prosecution offers (1) a witness who testifies that the victim has a reputation as a peaceful person, (2) a witness who testifies that the defendant has a reputation for violence, and (3) a bartender who testifies that the defendant broke a man’s jaw in a bar fight last year. The defendant didn’t offer evidence of his own character. Which rebuttal evidence is admissible?
o: Items 1 and 2 only.
Item 1 only, because the defendant never put his own character in issue.
Items 1, 2, and 3, because the defendant opened the door to violence.
None of them, because only a homicide victim’s peacefulness may be offered by the prosecution.
e: Rule: 404(a)(2)(B): if the accused offers the victim’s pertinent trait, the prosecution may rebut it and offer the accused’s same trait, by reputation or opinion only (405(a)).
oe: Correct. Once the defendant offers the victim’s pertinent trait under 404(a)(2)(B), the prosecution may (i) rebut it and (ii) offer evidence of the defendant’s same trait, even though he never offered his own character (the 2000 amendment). Under 405(a) both must be by reputation or opinion. Item 3 is a specific instance offered on direct, which 405(a) doesn’t allow.
404(a)(2)(B)(ii) was added in 2000 precisely so that an accused who attacks the victim’s trait opens the door to the same trait in himself.
Opening the door doesn’t change the method of proof. Specific acts come in only on cross of a character witness, or where character is an essential element under 405(b).
That describes 404(a)(2)(C), which lets the prosecution go first in a homicide case. In any criminal case, once the defendant offers the victim’s trait, 404(a)(2)(B) lets the prosecution respond.

q: A cyclist sues a delivery-van driver for negligence. The defense calls an accident-reconstruction expert who testifies that the cyclist ran a stop sign. On cross-examination, the plaintiff seeks to ask the expert whether he has been retained and paid in more than forty cases by the driver’s liability insurer, which is funding the defense. The defense objects under Rule 411. How should the court rule?
o: Overrule the objection, because Rule 411 permits insurance evidence offered to show a witness’s bias.
Sustain the objection, because Rule 411 bars any mention of liability insurance in front of the jury.
Sustain the objection, because a witness’s credibility may be attacked only by reputation or opinion under Rule 608.
Overrule the objection, because the jury is entitled to know the defendant can pay any judgment.
e: Rule: 411: insurance can’t prove negligence or wrongdoing, but may show bias, agency, ownership, or control (subject to 403).
oe: Correct. 411 bars insurance evidence only when offered to prove that a person acted negligently or otherwise wrongfully. An expert’s ongoing financial relationship with the insurer paying for the defense is classic bias, and here, unlike the adjuster in Lacher v. Anderson, it has real probative force.
411’s second sentence expressly allows insurance evidence for other purposes, including proving a witness’s bias or prejudice, agency, ownership, or control.
608 governs attacks on character for truthfulness. Bias is a separate, non-character mode of impeachment that may be shown on cross and by extrinsic evidence (Abel).
That is the forbidden inference: insurance used to suggest that liability or a large award is painless. The evidence comes in only for bias, and the defense may get an instruction saying so.

q: A defendant is charged with knowingly receiving 500 stolen laptops, which he bought for $40 each from a man in a parking lot. To prove he knew they were stolen, the government offers evidence that two months earlier he sold 200 new smartphones at a sixth of their retail price, from the same supplier, with no receipts or bill of sale. The government has no direct proof that the phones were stolen. What standard does the judge apply in deciding whether the jury may hear about the phone sales?
o: The judge asks whether a jury could reasonably find, by a preponderance, that the phones were stolen.
The judge must herself find by a preponderance under Rule 104(a) that the phones were stolen.
The judge must find by clear and convincing evidence that the phones were stolen.
The judge must exclude it unless the government proves beyond a reasonable doubt the phones were stolen.
e: Rule: Huddleston: other-act evidence comes in if a jury could reasonably find, by a preponderance, that the act occurred and the defendant did it (104(b)). Then 403 and 105 apply.
oe: Correct. Huddleston holds that whether the other act happened, here that the goods were stolen, is a question of conditional relevance under 104(b). The judge looks at all the evidence and asks whether a jury could reasonably find the fact. Low price, large quantity, and no bill of sale were enough in Huddleston itself.
Huddleston rejected a 104(a) finding by the judge. The judge doesn’t weigh credibility or make the finding; she asks only whether a reasonable jury could.
Some states once used a clear-and-convincing standard, but the federal rule after Huddleston is 104(b) sufficiency.
The other act is not a charged offense. Even an acquittal doesn’t bar other-act evidence (Dowling), because the 104(b) standard is far lower.

q: A driver is killed when a train hits her car at a rural crossing with no gates. In her estate’s wrongful-death suit, the railroad offers (1) a coworker’s testimony that, riding with her to work twice a day for five years, he saw her cross those tracks hundreds of times without ever slowing or looking, and (2) her sister’s testimony that she was “a careless, distracted driver in general.” No one saw the crash. Which testimony is admissible to show how she drove that day?
o: Item 1 only, as evidence of habit.
Neither, because character evidence can’t be used to prove conduct in a civil case.
Both, because in a wrongful-death case the decedent’s carefulness is an essential element under Rule 405(b).
Item 1 only, but only because no eyewitness saw the crash.
e: Rule: 406: habit (a specific, regular, semi-automatic response) is admissible to prove conduct, with or without an eyewitness or corroboration. General traits are 404(a) character.
oe: Correct. 406 admits a person’s habit to prove conduct on a particular occasion. Habit is a specific, regular, semi-automatic response to a repeated situation, like crossing the same tracks the same way hundreds of times (compare Halloran’s regular use of a coil). Item 2 is a general trait offered to prove conduct in conformity, which 404(a)(1) bars.
That is true of item 2, but habit isn’t character. 406 is a separate rule that applies in civil and criminal cases.
Carefulness is relevant to negligence, but character isn’t an essential element of the claim, as it would be in negligent entrustment or defamation.
406 says habit evidence may be admitted “regardless of whether it is corroborated or whether there was an eyewitness.” The lack of an eyewitness isn’t a requirement.

q: A federal agent is the only witness who saw the defendant toss a gun. The defense offers (1) a criminal defense lawyer who will testify that the agent has a bad reputation for truthfulness in the “courthouse community,” based on talks with three other defense lawyers, and that in his own opinion the agent is a liar because the agent testified against his clients; and (2) cross-examination of the agent about his failure to disclose a bankruptcy on his security-clearance form. The defense’s only support for item 2 is a credit-bureau printout that would itself be inadmissible hearsay. Which rulings fall within the court’s discretion?
o: Excluding the defense lawyer’s testimony for lack of foundation, while allowing the cross-examination.
Barring the cross-examination, because the defense has no admissible proof that the agent omitted the bankruptcy.
Admitting both and allowing the defense to introduce the credit-bureau printout if the agent denies the omission.
Excluding both, because character for truthfulness may be proved only by reputation.
e: Rule: 608(a) witnesses need an adequate foundation (Whitmore). 608(b) cross requires only a good-faith basis, and no extrinsic evidence is allowed.
oe: Correct. Whitmore upheld excluding character witnesses whose knowledge of the reputation was too thin or too remote, and the lawyer here spoke with only a few colleagues and based his opinion on testimony against his own clients. But 608(b) cross needs only a good-faith basis, not admissible proof, and omitting a bankruptcy on an official form is probative of untruthfulness. Barring that cross was the reversible error in Whitmore, where the officer was the key witness.

Whitmore rejected exactly this reasoning. The questioner needs only a reasonable, good-faith basis. The bar on extrinsic evidence means the defense must take the agent’s answer, not that it can’t ask.
608(b) forbids extrinsic evidence of specific instances offered to attack character for truthfulness. The defense may ask but can’t prove the omission with the printout.
608(a) permits opinion as well as reputation, and 608(b) separately permits cross about specific instances probative of untruthfulness.

q: In a federal prosecution of a physician for sexually abusing two patients during examinations, the government gives timely notice that it will offer four other patients’ testimony that he abused them the same way. The district judge excludes the testimony, explaining: “Evidence of other sexual assaults is always intensely prejudicial, so in Rule 413 cases I start with a strong presumption against admission.” The government appeals. What should the appellate court conclude?
o: The judge erred, because Rule 413 evidence gets an ordinary Rule 403 balance, with no presumption against it.
The judge was right, because Rule 413 evidence is presumptively inadmissible absent special need.
The judge erred, because Rule 403 doesn’t apply to evidence offered under Rule 413.
The judge was right, because Rule 413 requires that the other assaults have resulted in convictions.
e: Rule: Guardia: the 413 threshold (accused of sexual assault, evidence of another, relevance), then an ordinary 403 balance with no thumb on the scale.
oe: Correct. Guardia sets a threshold (sexual-assault charge, evidence of another sexual assault, relevance) and then requires a normal 403 weighing. Treating propensity as inherently too prejudicial would frustrate Congress’s purpose. In Guardia itself, exclusion was affirmed because of a specific risk of confusion: four more incidents with dueling experts on medical propriety. A judge may exclude for reasons like that, but not by presumption.
No such presumption exists. The rule says the court “may admit” the evidence “on any matter to which it is relevant,” including propensity.
403 applies to 413 evidence. Mound relied on that safeguard to uphold the rule against a due-process challenge.
Uncharged acts qualify. The standard of proof is presumably Huddleston’s, whether a jury could reasonably find the acts occurred.

q: In an armed-robbery trial, a prosecution eyewitness identifies the defendant. On cross, defense counsel asks, “Isn’t it true you’ve been dating the store owner’s daughter for the past year?” The witness answers, “No.” The defense later calls the daughter to testify that she and the witness have been dating for a year. The prosecution objects. How should the court rule?
o: Overrule the objection, because bias may be proved by extrinsic evidence after the witness denies it.
Sustain the objection, because Rule 608(b) bars extrinsic evidence of a witness’s specific conduct.
Sustain the objection, because the defense must take the witness’s answer on a collateral matter.
Overrule the objection, but only if the daughter testifies in the form of opinion or reputation.
e: Rule: Bias impeachment is non-character and never collateral, so extrinsic evidence is allowed after a denial (Abel).
oe: Correct. A relationship giving the witness a reason to shade testimony is bias, a non-character mode of impeachment. Abel holds that bias may be proved by extrinsic evidence, and 608(b)’s extrinsic-evidence bar doesn’t apply because the defense isn’t attacking character for truthfulness (Problem 4.8(2)).
608(b) applies only to conduct offered to show character for truthfulness. Bias works like 404(b) motive, around the box, so 608(b) is irrelevant.
The common-law collateral-matter rule never reached bias. A motive to favor the prosecution’s side bears directly on how much weight to give the identification.
Bias isn’t a character trait, so 608(a)’s opinion-or-reputation limit doesn’t apply. The daughter may testify to the specific fact of the relationship.

q: A defendant is on trial in 2026 for aggravated assault. If he testifies, the government wants to impeach him with his 2013 felony conviction for aggravated assault. He was released from prison in 2019. Which statement about the conviction’s admissibility is correct?
o: Rule 609(a)(1)(B) applies, because the ten years run from his 2019 release, and the crimes’ similarity weighs against admission.
Rule 609(b) applies because the conviction is more than ten years old, so the government must show probative value substantially outweighing prejudice.
The conviction must be admitted, subject only to Rule 403, because aggravated assault is punishable by more than a year.
The conviction must be admitted without balancing, because a violent felony bears on whether the defendant will respect his oath.
e: Rule: 609(b)’s ten years run from the later of conviction or release (Brewer). For an accused, 609(a)(1)(B) applies, weighed with the Gordon factors: nature of the crime, time and later history, similarity, importance of the defendant’s testimony, and centrality of credibility.
oe: Correct. 609(b)’s ten-year clock runs from the conviction or release from confinement, whichever is later (Brewer), so 609(b) doesn’t apply. Under 609(a)(1)(B), probative value on truthfulness must outweigh prejudice to the defendant. Among the Gordon factors, violent crimes say little about honesty, and a conviction for the same crime invites “he did it before” reasoning, so both point toward exclusion.
That was Brewer’s losing argument. The later of conviction or release starts the clock, and release in 2019 puts the conviction within ten years.
403’s lenient standard under 609(a)(1)(A) is for witnesses other than the accused. A testifying defendant gets the stricter 609(a)(1)(B) balance.
Only 609(a)(2) crimes, those requiring proof of a dishonest act or false statement, come in automatically. Assault isn’t one of them.
topic: Prior convictions (609) — FRE 609(b) · Brewer · Gordon factors

q: In a state rape prosecution, the defendant admits intercourse and claims it was consensual. His theory is that the complainant invented the rape because her live-in boyfriend saw her getting out of the defendant’s car and she feared he would leave her. The trial court, applying the state’s rape-shield law, bars all evidence that she lived with the boyfriend, even after she testifies that she lives with her mother. The defendant is convicted. On review, what is the strongest ruling?
o: The exclusion violated the Confrontation Clause by barring proof of a key witness’s motive to fabricate.
The exclusion was proper, because cohabitation is “other sexual behavior” and rape-shield laws have no exception for bias.
The exclusion was proper, because the defendant could argue the motive to lie in closing without introducing evidence of the relationship.
The exclusion was improper only if the defendant showed that her cohabitation made it more likely she consented.
e: Rule: 412(b)(1)(C) and Olden: excluding evidence of a prototypical motive to fabricate violates the Confrontation Clause, shield law or not.
oe: Correct. This is Olden v. Kentucky. The defendant’s theory was bias, a motive to lie, not her sexual character. Her testimony was central and was corroborated only by the possibly biased boyfriend, and her false claim to live with her mother made the need sharper. FRE 412(b)(1)(C) codifies this constitutional floor.
Shield laws must yield where exclusion would violate the defendant’s constitutional rights (412(b)(1)(C); Olden; Davis v. Alaska). Showing bias is at the core of confrontation.
Argument without evidence is no substitute for cross-examination. The jury needed the facts from which it could infer bias.
That would be the forbidden inference, sexual history used to prove consent. The evidence was admissible for a different reason: motive to fabricate.
topic: Rape shield (412) — FRE 412(b)(1)(C) · Olden v. Kentucky

q: A truck driver is charged under a state statute that makes it a crime to “transport any oysters harvested from closed waters.” The state’s highest court has held that the offense requires no proof of knowledge. The driver wants to testify that the crates were sealed when he picked them up and that he had no idea where the oysters were harvested. The prosecution objects. How should the court rule?
o: Sustain the objection, because his knowledge isn’t a fact of consequence under the statute.
Overrule the objection, because the testimony makes his innocence more probable.
Overrule the objection, because a criminal defendant always has the right to explain his conduct.
Sustain the objection, because the testimony’s probative value is substantially outweighed by the danger of confusing the issues.
e: Rule: 401(b) materiality comes from the substantive law. Evidence about a fact the law makes irrelevant is excluded by 402 (Egelhoff).
oe: Correct. Materiality comes from the substantive law. If the crime requires no knowledge, his ignorance doesn’t make any element more or less probable, and 402 excludes irrelevant evidence (compare Problem 1.4, Knowledge; Egelhoff).
Probativeness counts only if it bears on a fact of consequence. Under a no-knowledge offense, the driver’s ignorance doesn’t bear on any element.
A defendant has a right to present a defense, but not to offer evidence irrelevant to any element or defense recognized by the substantive law.
403 weighs relevant evidence. Here the evidence fails at the threshold under 401(b), materiality, so the court never reaches 403.

q: A rider is burned when an e-bike battery overheats. She sues the manufacturer on a strict-liability design-defect theory. The manufacturer concedes that a thermal cutoff switch was technologically and economically feasible but argues the original design was reasonable. The plaintiff offers (1) evidence that after her accident the manufacturer redesigned the battery to add a thermal cutoff, and (2) evidence that after her accident a national retailer, which isn’t a party, pulled the model from its shelves and posted warnings. How should the court rule?
o: Exclude item 1, but item 2 isn’t barred by Rule 407, though the court may weigh it under Rule 403.
Admit both, because Rule 407 doesn’t apply to claims brought on a strict-liability theory.
Exclude both, because Rule 407 bars every post-accident measure concerning the product.
Admit item 1, because it shows that a thermal cutoff was a feasible precaution.
e: Rule: 407 applies to product-defect claims (1997 amendment). Feasibility is a permitted purpose only if disputed. Most circuits: non-party measures aren’t barred by 407, though 403 still applies.
oe: Correct. Since 1997, 407 expressly covers measures offered to prove a defect in a product or its design, and feasibility isn’t disputed, so the redesign can’t come in that way. Most circuits hold that 407 doesn’t reach measures by non-parties (Millennium Partners), since third parties won’t be deterred from repairing. Their measures say little about this defendant, though, so some courts exclude them under 403.
Some pre-1997 decisions held that, but the amendment added “a defect in a product or its design” and “a need for a warning or instruction” to 407’s list.
407’s rationale, encouraging the defendant to repair, has little force for non-parties, and most courts don’t apply it to them.
Feasibility is a permitted purpose only “if disputed.” The manufacturer conceded it, so feasibility can’t serve as a backdoor.
topic: Remedial measures (407) — FRE 407 · product defect · non-parties

q: After a federal fraud conviction, the defendant moves for a new trial. He offers (1) a juror’s affidavit that several jurors drank vodka at lunch throughout the trial and dozed through afternoon testimony, and (2) testimony from a deputy marshal who saw one juror asleep during afternoon testimony and smelled alcohol in the jury box. Which evidence may the court consider?
o: The deputy marshal’s testimony, but not the juror’s affidavit.
Neither, because both concern the jury’s conduct during the trial.
Both, because drugs and alcohol are an “outside influence” under Rule 606(b)(2)(B).
Both, because drinking at lunch happened outside deliberations, so Rule 606(b) doesn’t apply.
e: Rule: Tanner: juror intoxication is internal, so juror testimony about it is barred. Nonjuror evidence (court personnel) remains available.
oe: Correct. Tanner held that juror intoxication is internal, no more an “outside influence” than a virus, poor food, or lack of sleep, so 606(b) bars juror testimony about it. But 606(b) limits only jurors. Nonjuror evidence, such as observations by courtroom personnel, remains one of the safeguards Tanner pointed to, along with voir dire, observation during trial, and jurors’ reports before the verdict.
606(b) restricts juror testimony and affidavits. It doesn’t bar a deputy’s own observations, which the district court in Tanner invited.
The Tanner majority rejected that reading. An outside influence means things like a bribe, a threat, or outside contact, not what jurors consume.
That was the Tanner dissent’s view. The majority, relying on the legislative history (the Senate version was enacted), held the juror testimony barred.

q: In a robbery trial, witnesses saw the robber flee in a green pickup with a ladder rack, driven by a man with a red beard and a neck tattoo. The prosecution calls a statistics professor who, using estimates he says are “reasonable” (one in 10 trucks is green, one in 20 has a ladder rack, one in 15 men has a red beard, one in 25 has a neck tattoo), multiplies the figures and testifies that there is only a 1-in-75,000 chance that a random man would match. The defendant matches. What is the defense’s best objection?
o: The figures are invented and may not be independent, and they invite the jury to equate a rare description with guilt.
Statistical evidence offered to prove identity is inadmissible as a matter of law after People v. Collins.
None, because experts may rely on reasonable estimates, and any weakness goes to weight, not admissibility.
The testimony is irrelevant because the defendant has no burden to prove someone else committed the crime.
e: Rule: Collins: probability evidence needs a foundation (real data, independent factors) and can’t turn a description’s rarity into a probability of guilt. Probabilistic evidence isn’t barred per se (DNA).
oe: Correct. That was People v. Collins: no foundation (made-up probabilities and non-independent factors, as a moustache is a subset of a beard) and distraction. A 1-in-75,000 description says nothing about whether this matching man, rather than another, was the robber, and an impressive expert can overwhelm the jury’s own weighing.
Collins doesn’t bar probabilistic evidence. DNA match statistics are routinely admitted (People v. Turner), and market-share liability rests on probabilities. The problem is foundation and misuse.

When the numbers have no evidentiary basis and the method assumes an independence it can’t show, the testimony lacks an adequate foundation. Its danger of misleading the jury also warrants 403 exclusion.
That confuses burdens with relevance. The real issues are foundation and the misleading leap from a description’s rarity to the probability of guilt.
topic: Rule 403 and 105 — People v. Collins · probability evidence

q: Three banks are robbed by a man wearing a rubber mask of a former president. Each time he hands the teller a note written on the back of a deposit slip from a different bank and leaves a single red carnation on the counter. Identity is disputed. The prosecution offers the defendant’s conviction for a robbery six years earlier in which he wore the same kind of mask, used the same kind of note, and left a red carnation. How should the court rule?
o: Admit it to prove identity, because the shared features are distinctive enough to amount to a signature.
Exclude it, because identity isn’t one of the exceptions to the propensity ban, so similar crimes stay out.
Admit it as propensity evidence, because the crimes are so similar that he is likely to repeat them.
Exclude it, because the earlier robbery is more than five years old and therefore too remote to be probative.
e: Rule: 404(b) identity: signature-level similarities (“could not be anyone else’s”) are admissible, subject to 403 and a 105 instruction (Trenkler).
oe: Correct. Modus operandi evidence proves identity when the similarities are idiosyncratic, so the crime “could not be anyone else’s” (Trenkler). A president mask, a note on another bank’s deposit slip, and a carnation together are a signature, not a prosaic commonality. The court then applies 403, weighing need, the strength of the similarity, how inflammatory the evidence is, and the risk of propensity reasoning, and gives a 105 instruction.
Identity is a permitted non-character purpose under 404(b)(2). The inference here is “this is his signature,” not “he is the robbing type.”
That is the forbidden inference. The evidence is admissible only because the signature points to the same person, and the jury should be told not to use it to infer criminal character.
No fixed time limit governs 404(b). Remoteness reduces probative value in the 403 balance, but six years doesn’t erase a signature this distinctive.
topic: Other acts (404(b)) — FRE 404(b) · modus operandi · Trenkler

q: A defendant charged with assault calls a witness who testifies that the defendant has a reputation in the community as a peaceful, nonviolent person. On cross-examination, with a good-faith basis, the prosecutor asks, “Have you heard that four years ago the defendant was arrested for shoplifting?” Defense counsel objects. How should the court rule?
o: Sustain the objection, because a shoplifting arrest isn’t relevant to a reputation for peacefulness.
Overrule the objection, because once a defendant offers character evidence, the prosecutor may ask about any prior arrest.
Sustain the objection, because a character witness may be asked only about convictions, not arrests.
Overrule the objection, and if the witness says he hasn’t heard of it, the prosecutor may prove the arrest with the police report.
e: Rule: 405(a) cross: the specific instance must be relevant to the trait the character witness addressed, the questioner needs a good-faith basis, and there’s no extrinsic proof.
oe: Correct. 405(a) allows cross-examination about “relevant specific instances,” which test the basis of the witness’s testimony about the pertinent trait. The witness vouched only for peacefulness, which a shoplifting arrest doesn’t contradict. In Michelson the witnesses had vouched for the defendant as honest and law-abiding, so a receiving-stolen-goods arrest was fair game; here the trait is narrower.
Opening the door to a trait doesn’t open the door to everything. The specific instance must be relevant to the trait the witness addressed.
Michelson allowed a question about an arrest: “it is not the man he is, but the name that he has which is put in issue.” An arrest can affect reputation.
Even when a question is proper, the cross-examiner must take the answer. Extrinsic proof of the specific instance isn’t allowed.
topic: Character and habit (404(a), 405, 406) — FRE 405(a) · relevant specific instances

q: A passenger sues both drivers involved in a three-car crash. Before trial, Driver B settles with the passenger for $60,000, and the settlement requires B to cooperate with the passenger at trial. B then testifies for the passenger that Driver A ran the red light. On cross-examination, Driver A wants to bring out the settlement and B’s cooperation obligation. How should the court rule?
o: Allow it, because Rule 408 permits compromise evidence offered to prove a witness’s bias.
Exclude it, because Rule 408 bars compromise evidence “on behalf of any party.”
Exclude it, because settlements between a plaintiff and one defendant may never be disclosed to the jury.
Allow it, because B’s willingness to pay $60,000 is evidence that B was at fault in the crash.
e: Rule: 408(b): compromise evidence may show a witness’s bias or prejudice, negate undue delay, or prove obstruction. It can’t prove validity or amount or impeach by prior inconsistent statement or contradiction.
oe: Correct. 408 bars compromise evidence only when offered to prove or disprove the validity or amount of a disputed claim, or to impeach by prior inconsistent statement or contradiction. Proving bias is expressly permitted. A settlement that obliges B to help the passenger gives B a reason to shade testimony.
That phrase addresses who may not offer compromise evidence for a prohibited purpose. It doesn’t override 408(b)’s permitted purposes, which include bias.
Courts may exclude third-party settlements when that serves settlement policy (Bradbury), but no absolute bar exists, and bias of a testifying settling party is a classic permitted use.
Using a settlement to prove liability is exactly what 408(a) prohibits. The only proper use here is to show bias.
topic: Compromise and medical expenses (408, 409) — FRE 408(b) · bias · settling co-defendant

q: A corporate executive is charged with fraud. Before trial, prosecutors offered him immunity if he would testify about wrongdoing by his business partner. He refused, saying, “I can’t tell you about crimes I don’t know about.” At trial, the government offers evidence that he bought gold coins right after his partner pleaded guilty, as consciousness of guilt. The executive offers his rejection of the immunity offer as consciousness of innocence. The government objects under Rule 410. How should the court rule?
o: Overrule the objection, because Rule 410 bars such evidence only when it is offered against the defendant.
Exclude it, because Rule 410 makes evidence of plea and immunity discussions inadmissible for all purposes.
Exclude it, because immunity negotiations are statements made in plea discussions with an attorney for the prosecuting authority.
Admit it, because the government waived Rule 410’s protection by offering immunity.
e: Rule: 410 protects only the defendant (“against the defendant”). A defendant may offer his rejection of immunity as consciousness of innocence (Biaggi), subject to 403.
oe: Correct. This is United States v. Biaggi (Mariotta). 410 bars evidence “against the defendant who made the plea or participated in the plea discussions.” Rejecting immunity, which would have cost him nothing if he knew of wrongdoing, is strongly probative of innocence, more so than rejecting a plea to a lesser charge. Allowing the government’s gold-coin evidence while barring his response was unfair.
410 is unusually broad, but by its text it protects only the defendant. It isn’t a general bar on offers made by the prosecution.
Even if the immunity talks count as plea discussions, 410 bars them only against the defendant. Here the defendant is offering his own conduct.
Waiver (Mezzanatto) is something a defendant does by agreement. The result here turns on 410’s “against the defendant” language, not on any waiver by the government.

q: A defendant charged with murder offers no character evidence. He testifies that the victim lunged at him with a box cutter and that he fired in self-defense. In rebuttal, the prosecution calls a witness who testifies that the victim had a reputation in his neighborhood as a peaceful man. The defense objects that it never offered evidence of the victim’s character. How should the court rule?
o: Overrule the objection, because evidence that a homicide victim struck first lets the prosecution offer his peacefulness.
Sustain the objection, because the prosecution may offer a victim’s character only after the defendant offers evidence of the victim’s character.
Overrule the objection, but only if the witness describes specific peaceful acts of the victim.
Sustain the objection, because the prosecution may never initiate character evidence in a criminal case.
e: Rule: 404(a)(2)(C): in a homicide case, the prosecution may offer the victim’s peacefulness to rebut any evidence that the victim was the first aggressor.
oe: Correct. 404(a)(2)(C) is the one prosecution-initiated character route outside 413–415. It is triggered by any evidence that the homicide victim was the first aggressor, including the defendant’s own testimony, not just by defense character evidence. The method is still reputation or opinion under 405(a).
That describes 404(a)(2)(B). Subsection (C) is broader in homicide cases: evidence that the victim struck first, whatever its form, opens the door.
405(a) limits proof to reputation or opinion. The witness’s reputation testimony is the right form.
404(a)(2)(C) is an exception that lets the prosecution offer the homicide victim’s peacefulness once first aggression is claimed.
topic: Character and habit (404(a), 405, 406) — FRE 404(a)(2)(C) · homicide victim

q: Police stop a car and find a handgun under the driver’s seat. The driver, a convicted felon, is charged with unlawful possession. He offers evidence that his passenger was convicted three years earlier of possessing a different handgun, arguing that it shows the gun was the passenger’s. The prosecution objects. How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because it shows only that the passenger tends to carry guns, which is propensity reasoning.
Admit it, because the propensity ban protects only criminal defendants, not third parties like the passenger.
Admit it, because Stevens applies a relaxed standard to any other-act evidence a defendant offers.
Exclude it, because a defendant may never offer evidence of another person’s crimes or bad acts.
e: Rule: Reverse 404(b) (Stevens): a lower similarity threshold and a 401 + 403 (waste, confusion) analysis, but still no propensity inference (Williams).
oe: Correct. This is Problem 3.10 (United States v. Williams, misreading Stevens). Reverse 404(b) evidence gets a lower similarity threshold, but the defense still must show a non-propensity inference, such as enough similarity to suggest that the same person committed both crimes (Stevens). A prior possession of a different gun shows only propensity.
404(b)(1) bars other-act evidence about “a person,” not just the defendant. Williams rejected the idea that Stevens licenses defense propensity evidence.
Stevens relaxed the degree of similarity needed (no “signature” required) and the 403 balance, but it didn’t drop the requirement of a non-propensity theory of relevance.
Reverse 404(b) evidence is admissible in a proper case. In Stevens, a similar robbery nearby whose victim said Stevens wasn’t the attacker was improperly excluded.

q: In a federal sexual-assault prosecution, the government gives timely notice that it will call a woman who will testify that the defendant raped her twelve years ago. He was tried for that incident in state court and acquitted. The defendant objects that (1) his acquittal bars the testimony and (2) Rule 413 violates due process by letting the jury convict him for who he is. How should the court rule on these objections?
o: Reject both: the acquittal doesn’t bar the evidence, and Rule 413 is constitutional because Rule 403 still applies.
Exclude the testimony, because admitting evidence of an acquitted charge violates double jeopardy.
Exclude the testimony, because Rule 413 applies only to sexual assaults that resulted in convictions.
Admit the testimony without further analysis, because Congress made sexual-assault propensity evidence admissible and Rule 403 doesn’t apply.
e: Rule: An acquittal doesn’t bar other-act evidence (Dowling: the Huddleston standard is lower). Mound upheld 413 because 403 still applies.
oe: Correct. The acquittal means only that guilt wasn’t proved beyond a reasonable doubt. Other-act evidence needs only enough for a jury to reasonably find, by a preponderance, that the act occurred (Huddleston; Dowling, Problem 3.14). Mound rejected the due-process challenge because 403 screens unfairly prejudicial evidence, and no court has held 413 or 414 unconstitutional. The judge must still weigh remoteness and the like under 403.
Dowling held that neither double jeopardy nor collateral estoppel bars such evidence, because the acquittal didn’t establish that the act didn’t happen under the lower standard.
413 reaches uncharged and unconvicted conduct; Rep. Molinari said so expressly.
403 applies to 413 evidence (Guardia), and it was the basis for upholding the rule in Mound.

q: A defense alibi witness testifies that he ate lunch with the defendant at a deli at the time of the robbery. Consider four things that happen on the prosecution’s cross-examination: (1) he admits he is in business with the defendant’s father; (2) he concedes the deli was closed that day and says they must have eaten next door; (3) he admits that he falsely claimed on a car-loan application that he had no other debts; (4) he admits that he and the defendant are close friends. After which of these may the defense offer evidence that the witness has a good reputation for truthfulness?
o: Item 3 only.
Items 1, 3, and 4.
Items 2 and 3.
All four, because each casts doubt on the witness’s credibility.
e: Rule: 608(a) rehabilitation is allowed only after a character attack (608(a), 608(b), or 609). Bias and a single contradiction don’t open the door.
oe: Correct. 608(a) allows support only after an attack on character for truthfulness. Lying on a loan application (a 608(b) act) is such an attack.
