Business ties and friendship show bias, which the ACN to 608(a) says isn’t a character attack, and a single contradiction usually isn’t one either (Problem 4.6).

Items 1 and 4 show a motive to favor the defendant. Bias suggests he is lying now for a reason, not that he is a liar, so it doesn’t open the door (compare Bonner, where the professor suggested “perhaps both courts erred”).
Exposing one contradiction is generally not an attack on character for truthfulness, though pervasive contradiction might be (ACN to 608(a): it “must depend upon the circumstances”).

Credibility can be attacked many ways, but only attacks on character for truthfulness, such as 608(a) opinion or reputation, 608(b) acts, and 609 convictions, open the door to good-character evidence.

q: In a civil contract suit, a key defense witness has three convictions: (1) a five-year-old felony assault conviction (punishable by up to three years); (2) a three-year-old misdemeanor conviction for filing a false police report (maximum 90 days); and (3) a two-year-old misdemeanor petty-theft conviction (maximum six months). The plaintiff offers all three to impeach. Which statement is correct?
o: Item 2 must be admitted, item 1 comes in unless Rule 403 calls for exclusion, and item 3 is out.
All three must be admitted, because theft and assault both reflect on the witness’s willingness to lie under oath.
Items 1 and 2 are admissible only if their probative value outweighs their prejudicial effect.
Item 2 is admissible only if it survives Rule 403, because misdemeanors always require balancing.
e: Rule: 609(a)(2) crimen falsi convictions must be admitted, with no balancing, whatever the punishment. 609(a)(1)(A) felonies offered against a non-accused witness are subject to 403. Theft isn’t crimen falsi.
oe: Correct. 609(a)(2) requires admitting any conviction whose elements required proving a dishonest act or false statement, and a false police report qualifies, with no 403 discretion. A felony offered against a witness in a civil case falls under 609(a)(1)(A), admitted subject to 403. Petty theft is a misdemeanor and isn’t crimen falsi, so neither branch applies.
Theft and robbery aren’t crimen falsi; the crime’s elements must require deceit or false statement. A misdemeanor theft therefore fits neither 609(a)(1) nor (a)(2).
That’s the 609(a)(1)(B) test for an accused. This witness isn’t a criminal defendant, and 609(a)(2) convictions aren’t balanced at all.

609(a)(2) applies “regardless of the punishment” and says the evidence “must be admitted.” Such convictions are “peculiarly probative” and always admitted, though 609(b)’s ten-year limit still applies.

q: A defense alibi witness is impeached with his five-year-old felony robbery conviction. The defense then calls the witness’s pastor, who testifies (1) that in his opinion the witness is a truthful person and (2) that the witness is a devout believer whose faith forbids lying. On cross-examination, the prosecutor, who has a good-faith basis, asks the pastor (3) whether he knows the witness lied on a mortgage application last year. Which items are proper?
o: Items 1 and 3.
Items 1 and 2.
Item 1 only, because a character witness can’t be asked about specific instances.
None of them, because a robbery conviction isn’t an attack on character for truthfulness.
e: Rule: 609 impeachment opens the door to 608(a) rehabilitation. 610 bars religious-belief evidence on credibility. 608(b)(2) lets cross probe the principal witness’s specific acts.
oe: Correct. The 609 conviction attacked the witness’s character for truthfulness, so 608(a) allows rehabilitation by opinion (item 1). Rule 610 bars evidence of religious beliefs to support or attack credibility (item 2). 608(b)(2) lets the cross-examiner ask a character witness about specific instances bearing on the truthfulness of the witness he vouched for, to test his opinion (Problem 4.6(4)). The prosecutor must take the pastor’s answer.
Item 2 uses the witness’s religious faith to bolster credibility, which Rule 610 forbids.
608(b)(2) expressly permits questions on cross about specific instances probative of the truthfulness of the witness whose character the character witness described.
Impeachment by a 609 conviction is an attack on character for truthfulness; that’s what 609 is for. It opens the door to 608(a) support.

q: A defendant is charged with molesting his 11-year-old stepdaughter, and there is no physical evidence. The defense wants to cross-examine her about an accusation she made two years ago that a music teacher touched her, which a classmate says she later admitted she “made up to get out of lessons.” The prosecution moves to exclude the cross-examination under the rape-shield rule. How should the court analyze the motion?
o: Rule 412 doesn’t apply; the court asks whether a jury could find the accusation false, then applies Rules 403 and 608.
Rule 412 bars the cross-examination, because the earlier accusation concerned sexual contact.
The defense may cross-examine only if the judge first finds by a preponderance that the earlier accusation was false.
The defense may cross-examine and, if she denies making it up, may call the classmate to prove the lie under Rule 608(b).
e: Rule: Prior false accusations aren’t “sexual behavior” (Smith; ACN), so they fall outside 412 and are governed by 608(b) and 403. Threshold: could a jury reasonably find the accusation false?
oe: Correct. State v. Smith held that past false allegations aren’t “past sexual behavior,” so the shield rule doesn’t bar them; the ACN to FRE 412 agrees. The question is impeachment, governed by 608(b) and 403. The threshold is Huddleston’s: whether reasonable jurors could find she made a false accusation, not whether the judge believes it was false (Problem 5.4).
412 bars evidence offered to prove a victim’s other sexual behavior or predisposition. A false accusation is offered to show she lies about such matters, not that she engaged in sexual behavior.
That is what the Smith trial judge effectively did, and it was error. The judge doesn’t decide falsity; she asks only whether a jury could reasonably find it.

608(b) permits inquiry on cross but bars extrinsic evidence of specific instances offered to attack character for truthfulness. The defense must take her answer unless some other theory, such as bias, applies.
topic: Rape shield (412) — Past false accusations · State v. Smith

q: In a federal civil trial, the jurors unanimously agree that the plaintiff’s damages are $85,000, but the foreperson writes “$8,500” on the verdict form. The verdict is read and the jury is discharged. Two days later, the foreperson tells the clerk about the mistake. Separately, the plaintiff learns that a juror who said in voir dire that she had no feelings about the defendant company failed to disclose that it had fired her brother. The plaintiff wants that juror’s fellow jurors to testify that during deliberations she said, “This company ruined my brother.” What may the court consider?
o: Juror testimony about the error on the verdict form, but not the testimony about the juror’s statement in deliberations.
Both, because voir-dire dishonesty is an exception to Rule 606(b).
Neither, because the verdict has been read and the jury discharged.
Only the deliberation statement, because it shows bias, while the form error concerns the jury’s mental processes.
e: Rule: 606(b)(2)(C): a juror may testify to a clerical mistake on the verdict form. Warger: deliberation testimony can’t prove voir-dire dishonesty (use other evidence).
oe: Correct. 606(b)(2)(C) lets a juror testify that a mistake was made in entering the verdict on the form, which fixes clerical errors without probing deliberations. Under Warger, juror testimony about deliberations can’t be used to show that a juror lied in voir dire. The plaintiff may try to make the Warger two-step showing (a dishonest answer to a material question, and a correct answer would have supported a for-cause challenge) with nonjuror evidence such as employment records.
Warger held the opposite: 606(b) applies even when the motion rests on voir-dire dishonesty, so deliberation statements can’t be used to prove it.
606(b)(2)(C) exists precisely to correct verdict-form errors discovered after the verdict.
Entering the wrong figure is a clerical mistake, not a mental process, and the text lets jurors testify to it. A statement made during deliberations is squarely within 606(b)(1)’s bar.

q: A warehouse worker charged with theft testifies that he was home asleep when the thefts occurred. He calls a polygraph examiner, who is barred from giving any test results, to testify that when she explained the machine and her high accuracy rate and asked if he wanted to proceed, he said, firmly and without hesitation, “Go ahead, hook me up. I’ve got nothing to hide.” The prosecution objects that the testimony is irrelevant. How should the court rule?
o: Overrule the objection, because his eagerness to take the test has some tendency to show consciousness of innocence.
Sustain the objection, because polygraph results are inadmissible, so anything connected to the test is irrelevant.
Sustain the objection, because the defendant’s own statements are self-serving and therefore irrelevant.
Overrule the objection, but only if the examiner also testifies that he passed.
e: Rule: 401’s “any tendency” bar is low. Willingness to submit to a test believed accurate is probative of consciousness of innocence; weakness goes to weight or 403.
oe: Correct. 401 sets a low bar: “any tendency.” A guilty person who believed the machine worked would be less likely to agree eagerly (Problem 1.3, Polygraph Consent; Stevens, J., dissenting in Scheffer). The weakness of the inference, since he may have known the results couldn’t be used, goes to weight or a 403 argument, not relevance.
The results are excluded, but the evidence here is his conduct and statement before the test, offered for a different inference.
Self-serving evidence isn’t irrelevant. Its weight is for the jury, and any hearsay issue is a different objection.
The results are barred. The consent evidence stands or falls on its own minimal probative value.

q: A hiker falls through a rotted footbridge on a trail and sues the state parks department. The department denies responsibility, claiming the bridge sits on land owned by a private conservation trust and that the department never maintained it. The plaintiff offers evidence that a week after the fall, a parks department crew replaced the bridge’s planks. How should the court rule?
o: Admit it to prove the department controlled the bridge, but not as proof of negligence.
Exclude it, because Rule 407 bars evidence of repairs made after an accident.
Admit it to prove negligence, because the department’s denial of control waived Rule 407’s protection.
Exclude it, because the “ownership or control” exception applies only in product-liability cases.
e: Rule: 407: subsequent measures are admissible to prove ownership or control if disputed, with a limiting instruction.
oe: Correct. 407 allows subsequent measures to prove ownership or control when disputed, and the department put control in issue by denying it. People generally repair what they control. The jury must be told not to treat the repair as an admission of fault.
407 bars repairs only when offered for the listed purposes, such as negligence. Disputed control is an express exception.
The denial makes control a permitted purpose. It doesn’t make the repair admissible to prove negligence.
The exception isn’t limited to product cases; it applies whenever ownership or control is disputed.

q: A woman charged with arson testifies on direct, “I would never set a fire. I’m just not that kind of person.” On cross-examination, the prosecutor, who has a fire-department report, asks, “Isn’t it true you set fire to your ex-boyfriend’s car two years ago?” Defense counsel objects. How should the court rule?
o: Overrule the objection, because by vouching for her own character she opened herself to cross on specific instances.
Sustain the objection, because she didn’t call a character witness, so her character isn’t in issue.
Sustain the objection, because Rule 608(b) limits cross-examination about specific acts to conduct probative of truthfulness.
Sustain the objection, because only her reputation, not her specific acts, may be raised on cross.
e: Rule: A defendant who vouches for her own trait becomes her own character witness, so cross about relevant specific instances is allowed (405(a); Problem 3.16).
oe: Correct. This is Problem 3.16 (“I Wouldn’t Shoot Anybody”). Her statement offered her own pertinent trait under 404(a)(2)(A), and 405(a) allows cross about relevant specific instances with a good-faith basis. The question also contradicts her testimony. The defense’s best move is a 105 instruction limiting how the jury uses her answer.
A defendant who testifies to her own good character has offered character evidence just as if she’d called a witness. She can’t vouch for herself and avoid cross on the same trait.
608(b) governs attacks on character for truthfulness. This cross tests her own testimony about a different trait (not setting fires) under 405(a), and it also contradicts her.
405(a) expressly allows inquiry into relevant specific instances of conduct on cross-examination of a character witness, which she became.
topic: Character and habit (404(a), 405, 406) — FRE 405(a) · I Wouldn’t Shoot Anybody (Problem 3.16)

q: Which of the following statements is admissible over a Rule 408 objection?
o: A chemical company’s admission to the EPA, made while negotiating to settle a civil enforcement action, offered in a later criminal prosecution for the same dumping.
A CEO’s statement at a settlement conference that “we knew the brakes were bad,” offered to impeach his trial testimony that the company had no reason to suspect a defect.
The same chemical company’s offer to pay a $2 million civil penalty, offered in the criminal prosecution to show consciousness of guilt.
A homeowner’s admission, during negotiations with his neighbor over a property-line dispute, that he knew he was building on her land, offered in a later criminal trespass prosecution.
e: Rule: 408(a)(2) exception: statements (not offers) made in negotiations with a public office are admissible in a later criminal case. 408 bars compromise statements used to impeach by prior inconsistent statement or contradiction.
oe: Correct. 408(a)(2) excludes statements made in compromise negotiations, “except when offered in a criminal case and when the negotiations related to a claim by a public office in the exercise of its regulatory, investigative, or enforcement authority.” A party talking to a regulator is on notice that its statements may be used by prosecutors.

Since 2006, 408 bars compromise statements offered “to impeach by a prior inconsistent statement or a contradiction.” That’s The Verdict clip: the bishop’s “tragic accident” can’t impeach his “act of God” testimony.

The criminal-case exception covers only conduct or statements under 408(a)(2). Offers to compromise under 408(a)(1) stay excluded even in criminal cases, since an offer may reflect a desire for peace.
The criminal-case exception applies only to negotiations with a public office exercising regulatory, investigative, or enforcement authority, not with a private party.
topic: Compromise and medical expenses (408, 409) — FRE 408(a) · public-office exception · impeachment

q: In a federal murder trial where the only issue is whether the defendant was the shooter, the prosecution calls the victim’s sister. It seeks to have her (1) show a photograph of the victim with his two young children at a birthday party and say briefly that he was a father of two who worked as a mechanic, and (2) testify that he “was the gentlest man alive and never got in a fight in his life.” The defense objects to both. Which ruling is most consistent with the rules as discussed in class?
o: Item 1 is within the court’s Rule 403 discretion, but item 2 is improper character evidence.
Both must be excluded as irrelevant, because the victim’s identity and death are undisputed.
Both are admissible under the “spark-of-life” doctrine, which lets the prosecution humanize the victim.
Item 2 is admissible under Rule 404(a)(2)(C), because in any homicide case the prosecution may prove the victim’s peaceful character.
e: Rule: Spark-of-life background is within 401/403 discretion. A victim’s peacefulness is character evidence, admissible only to rebut first-aggressor evidence (404(a)(2)(C)).
oe: Correct. Brief background that humanizes a victim, like the “spark-of-life” photo in the Chauvin trial, is left to the judge’s 401/403 discretion and is supported by Old Chief’s point about a morally reasonable verdict. But as Judge Cahill put it, propensity for peacefulness gets into character evidence. The prosecution may offer a homicide victim’s peacefulness only to rebut evidence that the victim struck first (404(a)(2)(C)), and identity is the only issue here.

The defense’s 401/403 objection to spark-of-life evidence is a real argument, but courts have discretion to allow brief humanizing background. Item 2 fails for a different reason: it’s character evidence.
Spark-of-life is a Minnesota doctrine (State v. Graham), and even there it doesn’t override the character rules. Item 2 is offered to show the victim’s peaceful nature.
404(a)(2)(C) applies only to rebut evidence that the victim was the first aggressor, which no one has offered here.

q: A trucking-company owner pleaded nolo contendere to a misdemeanor charge of falsifying drivers’ logbooks. In a separate case arising from a fatal crash involving one of his trucks, he pleaded guilty to reckless endangerment and did not withdraw the plea. He also pleaded guilty to a third charge but was later allowed to withdraw that plea. In the victim’s family’s wrongful-death suit against him, which is admissible against him?
o: His guilty plea to reckless endangerment.
His nolo contendere plea to falsifying logbooks.
The guilty plea he later withdrew.
His statements to the judge during the plea colloquy on the nolo plea.
e: Rule: 410 bars withdrawn guilty pleas, nolo pleas, and statements in those plea proceedings. A guilty plea that stands is admissible.
oe: Correct. 410 protects only withdrawn guilty pleas, nolo pleas, statements made in proceedings on those pleas, and statements in failed plea talks with a prosecutor. A guilty plea that stands is not protected and may be offered against him as his own statement.
410(a)(2) bars a nolo plea against the defendant in any later civil or criminal case. That protection is the main reason defendants enter nolo pleas.
410(a)(1) bars a guilty plea that was later withdrawn.
410(a)(3) bars statements made during a Rule 11 (or comparable state) proceeding on a nolo or later-withdrawn guilty plea.

q: A man is insulted in a bar and tells the other patron, “I’ll be back to settle this.” He returns forty minutes later and stabs the patron to death. At his trial for premeditated murder, the prosecution offers (1) a receipt showing he bought a hunting knife at an all-night store fifteen minutes after leaving the bar, and (2) testimony that police found a collection of twelve knives and a set of brass knuckles in his apartment, none used in the killing. How should the court rule?
o: Admit item 1 as preparation, but exclude item 2 as evidence of character.
Admit both, because the weapons collection shows he had the means to carry out his threat.
Exclude both, because evidence of weapons the defendant possessed is always unfairly prejudicial.
Admit item 2, because owning knives and brass knuckles isn’t a crime, so Rule 404(b) doesn’t apply.
e: Rule: 404(b): preparation, such as acquiring the weapon after the threat, is a permitted purpose. Unused weapons offered to show dangerous character are barred (Zackowitz).
oe: Correct. Buying a weapon right after the insult is preparation, a permitted purpose, as the Zackowitz court noted it would be if he had bought the guns after the insult. The weapons collection, never used, invites the inference Cardozo condemned, that he is “a desperate type of criminal,” and fails 404(b)(1) and 403.
That was the Zackowitz dissent’s argument, which the majority rejected. Owning other weapons adds little to the means question and a great deal of propensity prejudice.
The knife bought after the threat is strongly probative of premeditation, the vital question. 403 calls for exclusion only when unfair prejudice substantially outweighs probative value.
404(b) covers any “other crime, wrong, or act,” and 404(a) bars character evidence generally. Lawful possession offered to show a violent disposition is still propensity evidence.

q: A defendant charged with assault claims he punched the alleged victim in self-defense. He offers testimony from two strangers that the victim beat each of them in separate bar fights last year. The defendant didn’t know about either fight when he threw the punch. Under which theory, if any, is the testimony admissible?
o: None. Self-defense doesn’t make the victim’s character an essential element, and he didn’t know of the fights.
Rule 405(b), because a claim of self-defense puts the victim’s violent character directly in issue as an element.
Rule 404(a)(2)(B), which allows a defendant to prove the victim’s violent character by specific acts.
Rule 406, because two bar fights in one year show the victim’s habit of violence.
e: Rule: 405(b) allows specific acts only when character is an essential element (entrapment, truth in defamation, negligent entrustment, custody), not in self-defense. The victim’s violence comes in by reputation or opinion under 404(a)(2)(B).
oe: Correct. Under 404(a)(2)(B) the defendant may offer the victim’s violent trait, but 405(a) limits him to reputation or opinion. 405(b) allows specific instances only when the trait is an essential element, and self-defense turns on the defendant’s reasonable fear, not on the victim’s actual character. Because he didn’t know of the fights, there’s no state-of-mind route either (contrast James, where the records corroborated what the victim had told her). Offering even reputation evidence would open the door to his own violent character under 404(a)(2)(B)(ii).
The rule says “person,” and some argue the victim’s character is an element, but the element of self-defense is the defendant’s reasonable belief. Character is at most circumstantial.
404(a)(2)(B) allows the trait to be offered, but 405(a) controls the method: reputation or opinion on direct, specific instances only on cross.
Two fights aren’t a habit. Habit is a regular, semi-automatic response to a repeated situation, not a general disposition toward violence.

q: In a state whose evidence rules mirror the federal rules except that it has no counterparts to Rules 413–415, a youth swim coach is charged with sexually assaulting a 14-year-old team member. The prosecution offers testimony from two former team members that he groomed and assaulted them in the same way years earlier. It argues the evidence shows his (1) motive (sexual attraction to teenage swimmers), (2) intent, and (3) common plan. Under the reasoning of State v. Kirsch, how should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because each theory rests on propensity, and similar methods show a pattern, not a plan.
Admit it as evidence of a common plan, because he groomed and assaulted each victim in the same way.
Admit it as evidence of motive, because sexual attraction explains why he committed the charged assault.
Admit it under Rule 413, because state courts must follow the federal rules on sexual-assault propensity evidence.
e: Rule: Without 413–415, motive, intent, and plan labels can’t disguise sexual propensity (Kirsch). A plan requires an overall scheme, not a pattern.
oe: Correct. Kirsch rejected all three around-the-box theories. A desire to have sex with young girls “is proof of propensity, not motive.” The intent theory was “indistinguishable” from propensity. And “a pattern or systematic course of conduct is insufficient to establish a plan.” In federal court, by contrast, Rule 413 or 414 would let the evidence in for propensity, subject to 403.
Similar methods show a pattern, which Kirsch held insufficient. A true plan requires each act to be a constituent part of a larger scheme.
Kirsch saw through this label: the “motive” is just the propensity itself, described differently.
The Federal Rules of Evidence bind federal courts. States choose their own rules, and this state has no 413 counterpart.
topic: Sexual-assault propensity (413–415) — No 413 analog · State v. Kirsch

q: A pedestrian is struck by a car driven by a courier and sues a delivery company. The company denies that the courier was its agent, claiming he was an independent contractor who used his own car. The plaintiff offers evidence that the company paid the premiums on a commercial auto liability policy listing the courier as a covered driver. How should the court rule?
o: Admit it to prove agency or control, but not to show negligence.
Exclude it, because Rule 411 bars evidence that a party carried liability insurance.
Admit it, because it shows the company can easily pay any judgment the jury awards.
Exclude it, because insurance evidence is admissible only to show a witness’s bias.
e: Rule: 411 permits insurance evidence to prove agency, ownership, control, or bias.
oe: Correct. 411 bars insurance evidence offered to prove negligence or other wrongdoing, but it expressly permits insurance evidence to prove “agency, ownership, or control.” Paying to insure a driver tends to show the company treated him as its own. The court should still weigh 403 and give a limiting instruction.
411 bars insurance only for the forbidden purpose. Its second sentence lists permitted purposes, and agency is one of them.
That is precisely the risk 411 guards against: jurors awarding damages to whoever can pay.
Bias is one permitted purpose, but so are agency, ownership, and control.

q: A defendant is charged with a shooting outside a nightclub. The prosecution offers a video, recorded eight months before the shooting, of the defendant performing a song he wrote with lyrics about “riding with a nine” and “leaving opps on the pavement.” The lyrics mention no nightclub, no victim, and no detail of the charged shooting. The prosecution argues that they show his intent and motive. How should the court rule?
o: Exclude it, because lyrics with no link to the shooting show only violent character.
Admit it, because a defendant’s own words describing violence are evidence of his intent and motive.
Admit it, because the Federal Rules contain no special rule for creative expression.
Exclude it, because the First Amendment bars using creative expression as evidence.
e: Rule: Lyrics and other creative expression without specific links to the crime invite propensity reasoning, so 404(b) and 403 exclude them (Skinner; Bey-Cousin). Specific matching details may come in.
oe: Correct. This is Problem 3.5 (State v. Skinner): violent lyrics with no specific connection to the crime invite the jury to infer violent character, and the N.J. Supreme Court condemned their use. Bey-Cousin v. Powell presumes that “artists tell stories.” Lyrics describing details unique to the crime could come in to show intent (the HTGAWM clip), but these don’t.
Intent is a proper purpose only when the evidence bears on intent without running through character. Generic violent art, without specifics, is the kind of evidence Skinner found propensity-laden.
True, there is no federal statute like those in California, Louisiana, and Maryland, but that doesn’t make the lyrics admissible. They must still pass 404(b) and 403.
No absolute bar exists, even under the new state statutes. Sufficiently specific lyrics can be admitted, so exclusion here rests on 404(b) and 403.
topic: Other acts (404(b)) — Creative expression · State v. Skinner

q: At his 2026 trial for grand theft, the defendant testifies that he was out of state when the theft occurred. In 2022 he shot a man in the arm during a bar fight and was convicted of felony assault with a dangerous weapon. In 2024 he was convicted of misdemeanor turnstile jumping and served 30 days. The prosecutor proposes four ways to impeach him. Which may the court permit?
o: Evidence of the 2022 assault conviction, if it passes Rule 609(a)(1)(B)’s balancing test.
Cross-examination asking whether he shot a man in the arm during the 2022 bar fight.
Testimony from a bartender who saw him shoot the man in the arm during the 2022 fight.
Cross-examination asking whether he was convicted of turnstile jumping in 2024.
e: Rule: Impeaching an accused: felony convictions go through 609(a)(1)(B). 608(b) reaches only acts probative of truthfulness, on cross, with no extrinsic proof, and it isn’t a back door around 609.
oe: Correct. A felony conviction of a testifying accused is admissible under 609(a)(1)(B) if it passes that special balance. Violent crimes are weak on honesty, so admission isn’t guaranteed, but it’s the only route the rules allow among these options.
608(b) permits cross only about acts probative of truthfulness, and a shooting isn’t one. Asking about the underlying act would also be a back door around 609’s protections for convictions.
This is extrinsic evidence of a specific act. 608(b) bars it as proof of character for truthfulness, and offered to show violent character it’s propensity barred by 404.
A misdemeanor qualifies under 609 only if it is crimen falsi, which fare evasion isn’t, and it isn’t the kind of deceitful act 608(b) reaches either.

q: In a federal robbery trial, the defendant seeks to impeach a prosecution witness. Which of the following is most likely admissible?
o: A four-year-old felony assault conviction that is currently on appeal.
A juvenile adjudication for burglary from when the witness was fifteen, where the witness also has two adult felony convictions.
A felony conviction for which the witness later received a certificate of rehabilitation, with no later felony convictions.
A three-year-old misdemeanor conviction for drunk driving.
e: Rule: 609(c): a pardon or certificate based on rehabilitation or innocence bars the conviction. 609(d): juvenile adjudications only against a non-accused witness in a criminal case, and only if necessary. 609(e): a pending appeal doesn’t bar the conviction.
oe: Correct. A felony conviction of a witness other than the accused comes in under 609(a)(1)(A), subject to 403, and 609(e) provides that a pending appeal doesn’t make the conviction inadmissible (though evidence of the appeal is also admissible).

609(d) admits a juvenile adjudication of a non-accused witness in a criminal case only if it is necessary to fairly determine guilt or innocence. With two adult felonies available, it isn’t (as with the “reform school” question in the Anatomy of a Murder clip).
609(c)(1) bars a conviction that was the subject of a certificate of rehabilitation based on a finding of rehabilitation, if the person hasn’t been convicted of a later felony.
DUI is a misdemeanor and doesn’t require proof of a dishonest act or false statement, so it fits neither 609(a)(1) nor 609(a)(2).

q: An employee sues her former supervisor and employer for sexual harassment, seeking damages for emotional distress. She makes no claim of harm to her reputation. The defense moves, in a timely sealed filing, to offer (1) evidence that she had a consensual relationship with a coworker, to suggest she welcomed sexual banter in the office, and (2) testimony that she had a reputation around the office for promiscuity. Which ruling is correct?
o: Item 1 is admissible only if it passes Rule 412(b)(2)’s test, and item 2 is inadmissible.
Both are barred, because Rule 412 contains no exceptions at all in civil cases.
Both are admissible under ordinary Rule 403 balancing, because this is a civil case.
Item 1 is barred, because Rule 412(b)(1)(B) allows only sexual behavior with the accused.
e: Rule: 412(b)(2), civil cases: probative value must substantially outweigh harm to the victim and unfair prejudice to any party. Reputation comes in only if the victim placed it in controversy.
oe: Correct. 412(b)(2) reverses the usual 403 balance in civil cases: the evidence must substantially outweigh the danger of harm to any victim and of unfair prejudice to any party. Reputation evidence is admissible only if the victim has placed it in controversy (compare Jones v. Clinton, Problem 5.9, where her claim of reputational damage arguably did). This plaintiff hasn’t.
412(b)(2) supplies a civil exception, a weighing test heavily tilted against admission, but not an absolute bar.
Civil cases get a stricter test than 403: probative value must substantially outweigh harm and unfair prejudice. Reputation also requires that the victim put it in controversy.
412(b)(1) lists the criminal-case exceptions. Civil cases use 412(b)(2)’s balancing test instead.
